props.title: How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying
props.initialSlug: Ambitious window washer schemes his way to the top

sections.content: How to Succeed in Business Without Really Trying (1967) brilliantly translates the sharp-tongued satire of 1960s corporate culture from stage to screen. Robert Morse recreates his Tony-winning role as J. Pierrepont Finch, the window washer who schemes his way up the corporate ladder at World Wide Wickets. The film belongs to that golden age of movie musicals like The Music Man (1962) and Bye Bye Birdie (1963) that maintained theatrical energy while adding cinematic flair. Director David Swift captures the era's sleek modernist offices and Madison Avenue swagger with a knowing wink.

sections.content: The film's satirical bite feels remarkably fresh today, skewering corporate buzzwords, office politics, and shameless self-promotion. Scenes like "A Secretary is Not a Toy" and "Coffee Break" nail workplace dynamics that still ring true. The movie shares DNA with cynical corporate comedies like 9 to 5 (1980) and Office Space (1999), though its technicolor optimism and jazzy Frank Loesser score keep things bouncing along.

What sets this adaptation apart is how it maintains the theatrical staging while finding clever cinematic solutions. The fantasy sequence "I Believe in You" uses mirrors to multiply Finch's reflection, creating a surreal corporate hall of mirrors. Sweet Charity (1969) and All That Jazz (1979) would later push this theatrical-meets-cinematic style even further. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Corporate Satire

movies.title: The Wolf of Wall Street
movies.slug: Another tale of shameless corporate climbing, though with considerably more edge

sections.content: While How to Succeed plays corporate ambition for laughs, later films like Wall Street (1987) and Glengarry Glen Ross (1992) would tackle similar themes with dramatic intensity. The film's DNA lives on in corporate comedies like Working Girl (1988) and In Good Company (2004), though few maintain its perfect balance of satire and song.
